answers.java_tx_design: I owned the transaction boundary redesign on our booking-payments service. Originally a booking confirmation, the payment capture, and a loyalty-points write all happened in one transaction, and under a flash-sale spike that transaction would hold locks for up to 2 seconds because the loyalty write touched a hot points-balance row shared across many bookings. I split loyalty points into an async step consumed off a queue after the payment transaction commits, so the core booking transaction dropped to under 150ms even at peak. The failure that pushed this: the first version of the async split didn't handle a failed loyalty write at all, so a few dozen bookings silently never got points credited until we added a retry with dead-letter handling.
answers.java_ops: We had GC pauses on the booking-payments service — G1GC pauses around 600-900ms during checkout spikes — that showed up as timeout spikes on our payment gateway calls. I profiled with async-profiler and traced it to excessive allocation from building large intermediate booking objects on every request. Reworked the hot path to reuse builders instead of allocating fresh objects per request, and pauses dropped to under 150ms at the same load. Separately, we had connection pool exhaustion when a partner hotel's API started responding slowly during an outage on their end — I added a 3-second timeout and a circuit breaker, which kept our pool from being starved by their problem.
answers.rust_readiness: We've had a Rust service in production for about a year and a half — the payment-authorization hot path that used to be Java. We moved it because p99 latency on authorization was sitting around 280ms under peak checkout load, largely from GC pauses and JIT warmup variance, and for a payment flow that's real money to a hotel and a guest, that unpredictability mattered more than raw throughput. In Rust, p99 dropped to about 40ms with far less variance. Biggest failure: an early version used blocking I/O inside a tokio task for a downstream fraud-check call, which starved the runtime under load and caused a worse outage than the Java version ever had, until we fixed it to use the async client properly.
answers.rust_boundary: For the authorization service, Java kept booking and loyalty logic, and Rust owns just the authorization decision — fraud score plus a couple of payment-network calls — behind a gRPC boundary, with the result written back to the same Postgres ledger Java writes to, so there's one source of truth for the transaction record either way. Before migrating we baselined p99 latency, memory, and GC pause time on the Java version for a month; after, we tracked the same numbers plus a reconciliation job comparing authorization decisions between old and new paths during a two-week shadow period before Rust took real traffic.
answers.money_correctness: Our authorization service dedupes on an idempotency key built from booking ID plus attempt number, stored with a unique constraint, checked before any charge is attempted. It broke once during the fraud-check timeout issue I mentioned — a client retry came in with what looked like a new attempt number because our mobile app's retry logic didn't preserve the original one after a specific kind of network error, so 23 bookings got charged twice over about ninety minutes, roughly $6,800 total. I caught it from a spike in our duplicate-charge alert, which compares charge count to booking count per ID. We refunded the duplicates as new offsetting transactions, never edited the original charges, and fixed the mobile retry logic to preserve the attempt number.
answers.incident_response: That double-charge incident: alert fired at 2:14am, I confirmed the scope by 2:40 — 23 bookings, about $6,800 — and had the offsetting refunds processed by 4am, with guests seeing corrected balances by morning. I told my manager and our payments lead as soon as I'd confirmed the scope, around 2:45, well before I had the fix ready. The postmortem's fix was preserving the attempt number through app-level retries, which we shipped within three days, and I added an alert on the duplicate-charge ratio dropping from a daily check to real-time. It hasn't recurred in the year since.
answers.process_skipping: During that 2am incident I didn't skip review for the offsetting-refund script — I wasn't going to invent a new money-moving script at 2am without another set of eyes — but our incident process lets a second on-call engineer approve over a call instead of a full PR review, which is what happened, in under ten minutes. The permanent mobile-retry fix went through completely normal review a few days later. I've never pushed a change past procedure outside a declared incident — for something touching payments, the risk isn't worth whatever time it'd save.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: The double-charge incident is my mistake-sharing example too, in a sense — even though the bug was in the mobile app's retry logic, not mine, I told the team the exact moment I understood the scope rather than quietly fixing it first. I've done on-call for the payments team for the full four years I've been here, about one week in four, and I still take it now that I'm more senior — I think stepping back from it would be a bad signal. I also mentor one newer engineer, pairing weekly, mostly on reading postmortems and tracing incidents from alert to root cause.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a plan to add a second, independent fraud-check vendor purely to reduce false declines, without changing our decision logic. I ran our decline data against both vendors' outputs on the same three weeks of traffic and showed the actual overlap in what they'd catch was over 90%, meaning the second vendor mostly added cost and latency without meaningfully improving accuracy. The team dropped the second-vendor plan and tuned our existing thresholds instead, which I implemented, and once that was decided I didn't keep raising the vendor idea again.
answers.own_contribution: On the Rust authorization migration I described: the tokio blocking-I/O bug and its fix were entirely mine to diagnose and correct; the decision on the two-week shadow-traffic period length, and when we'd trust it enough to cut over, was made jointly with my tech lead and the fraud team, not just me. On the transaction-boundary redesign, splitting out the async loyalty-points write was my design; the decision to also change our loyalty program's crediting SLA from immediate to within-a-minute was a product call made with the loyalty team afterward.
answers.java_recovery: When loyalty points silently failed to credit after that early async-split bug, I scoped it with a query comparing completed bookings against loyalty-ledger entries for the same date range, which surfaced 34 bookings missing points over about two weeks before we caught it. I fixed it by crediting the missing points as new ledger entries dated at correction time, not backdating them, then cross-checked the total points issued against the total eligible booking value to confirm nothing else was missed.
answers.java_perf_change: I brought p99 latency on the booking confirmation endpoint from about 720ms to 190ms by finding the loyalty-points calculation was running synchronously inline even before I split it into the async step I mentioned — it was doing a full history recalculation instead of using a running balance. First fix attempt was just caching the loyalty balance, but balances change too often around a booking for a cache to stay correct, and it caused a couple of wrong point totals in testing, so I reverted it and moved to the async, running-balance approach instead.
answers.rust_hands_on: In the authorization service, I got stuck on a Send bound — I wanted to share a fraud-rules cache across worker tasks and pass a reference into a spawned tokio task, and the compiler wouldn't accept it because my cache used an Rc internally instead of an Arc. Once I understood that Rc isn't safe to share across threads and swapped it for Arc<RwLock<...>>, it compiled and worked, but I also had to fix the lock contention that came with it, moving to arc-swap so readers didn't block each other on every request.
answers.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move the booking-confirmation service itself — it changes with nearly every product launch, it's not the latency-sensitive piece, and rewriting it would mean re-verifying a dozen integrations for no real gain. I did hold back a full rewrite of the loyalty-points service, actually — I wanted to redo it in Rust after the authorization migration went well, but we measured that its latency was already fine and its change rate was too high for a small team to maintain two languages there, so we left it in Java and I dropped the idea.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: Separate from the double-charge incident: our nightly settlement once showed a $3,200 gap against a partner hotel chain. Traced it to a batch of cancellations processed at 11:57pm landing in the next day's settlement file because the partner's system used their local timezone for the cutoff while ours used UTC. Took about four hours to find, cross-referencing cancellation timestamps in both systems. We fixed it by aligning cutover logic to a single agreed timezone with that partner and corrected the affected day with a new entry rather than moving the original records.
answers.prod_data_verification: To verify the mobile-retry fix actually preserved attempt numbers correctly, I didn't test against real bookings — I replayed the exact network-error scenario from the incident against a staging environment seeded with masked production-shaped booking data, and confirmed the attempt number survived the retry. For the arc-swap fix in the authorization service, staging couldn't reproduce the concurrency pattern under real load, so I ran it as a shadow path in production — computing a result but not committing it — for about two hours, announced in our incident channel first, before trusting it with real traffic.
